title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A start-to-finish Docker series covering architecture, images and containers, Dockerfile and build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging and production orchestration, ending with a command cheat sheet and interview questions.

chapters.title: Docker Complete Handbook
points: Docker packages an app and its dependencies into an image that runs the same on any host
Series map: architecture, images, Dockerfile, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production
Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds and use far less memory than VMs

chapters.title: Docker Architecture and Internals
points: The client (docker CLI) talks over a REST API to dockerd, which delegates to containerd, which calls runc to create the container
Namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) isolate what a process sees; cgroups limit CPU, memory and I/O
Containers vs VMs: containers share the host kernel and are MBs in size; VMs boot a full guest OS and are GBs
Mistake: assuming a container is a security boundary as strong as a VM; a kernel exploit affects every container on the host

chapters.title: Images and Containers Lifecycle
points: An image is a read-only stack of layers; a container adds a thin writable layer on top via copy-on-write (overlay2)
Lifecycle states: created, running, paused, exited, removed, driven by create, start, stop, rm
docker stop sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL after 10s; docker kill sends SIGKILL at once
Mistake: storing data in the writable layer; it is lost on docker rm

chapters.title: Dockerfile and Build Optimization
points: Each instruction creates a layer; unchanged layers are served from the build cache until one changes, which invalidates everything after it
Order for cache hits: copy dependency manifests (package.json) first, install, then copy the source
Multi-stage builds: FROM node AS build, then COPY --from=build into a slim runtime image to drop build tools
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: CMD is the overridable default; ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable. Use exec form ["a","b"] so signals reach PID 1
A .dockerignore (node_modules, .git, .env) keeps the build context small and secrets out

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: Three mount types: named volume (managed by Docker), bind mount (host path), tmpfs (memory only)
Volumes live in /var/lib/docker/volumes, survive container removal and can be shared between containers
Volume vs bind mount: volumes are portable and driver-capable; bind mounts suit dev hot-reload but depend on host paths and permissions
Example: docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres keeps the database across restarts
Mistake: running docker volume prune or compose down -v, which deletes data silently

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Network drivers: bridge (default), host, none, overlay (multi-host) and macvlan
The default bridge has no DNS by container name; user-defined bridges resolve names automatically
-p 8080:80 publishes a container port on the host through iptables NAT rules
Example: docker network create app, then run api and db on it so that api reaches db at db:5432
Mistake: binding a service to 127.0.0.1 inside the container, which makes it unreachable from outside

chapters.title: Docker Compose for Multi-Container Apps
points: compose.yaml declares services, networks and volumes, and docker compose up starts the whole stack
Compose creates one default network per project, and services reach each other by service name
depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for a healthcheck; plain depends_on only controls start order
Profiles, override files and env_file configure dev vs prod from the same base file
Mistake: treating Compose as production orchestration; it runs on a single host with no self-healing across nodes

chapters.title: Registries and Image Tagging
points: A registry stores images by repository and tag; examples are Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR and a private registry:2
Push flow: docker build -t repo/app:1.4.2, then docker login, then docker push
Tags are mutable pointers; a digest (@sha256:...) is immutable, so pin digests for reproducible deploys
Mistake: relying on :latest, which does not mean newest and makes rollbacks ambiguous

chapters.title: Docker Security Best Practices
points: Run as a non-root user with USER in the Dockerfile; root in a container is root on the host if it escapes
Drop capabilities (--cap-drop ALL), use --read-only and --security-opt no-new-privileges
Minimal bases (alpine, distroless) shrink the attack surface; scan images with Trivy or docker scout
Mistake: baking secrets into ENV or layers, which stay in image history; use BuildKit secrets or runtime secret stores

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Containers
points: First checks: docker ps -a, docker logs -f --tail 100, docker inspect for config and State.ExitCode
docker exec -it c sh opens a shell in a running container; docker run --entrypoint sh debugs one that crashes at start
Exit codes: 137 means SIGKILL or OOM, 143 means SIGTERM, 1 means app error, 127 means command not found
docker stats and docker events show resource use and daemon activity
Mistake: a container exits at once because the main process is not in the foreground

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Production needs restart policies (unless-stopped), HEALTHCHECK, resource limits (--memory, --cpus) and log rotation
Orchestrators add scheduling, scaling, rolling updates and self-healing across hosts
Swarm vs Kubernetes: Swarm is simple and built in; Kubernetes has a larger ecosystem and more power, with more complexity
Mistake: unbounded json-file logs and missing memory limits, which fill the disk or trigger OOM kills

chapters.title: Docker Cheatsheet and Interview Questions
points: Containers: run -d --name -p -v -e, ps -a, stop, rm, exec -it, logs -f
Images: build -t, images, pull, push, tag, rmi, image prune, history
Cleanup and inspection: system prune, volume ls, network ls, inspect, stats
Interview: explain image vs container, CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, COPY vs ADD, and how a container differs from a VM
Interview: how do you shrink an image, persist data, make two containers talk, and secure a production container?
